Senses.Explanation: The two daily gruel-and-rice meals are the monastery’s fixed meal-times. Zhaozhou says that during forty years he had no mixed use of mind apart from these meals; later masters quote, challenge, and institutionalize that formula, including the right of ordained residents to receive them. Zhaozhou’s saying defines the recurring formula: apart from the two gruel-and-rice meals, he had no mixed use of mind. Lamp and instruction records repeatedly quote it. Wuzhun Shifan asks where Zhaozhou fell outside the two meals, then counters that when gruel comes one eats gruel and when rice comes one eats rice. Gaofeng Yuanmiao uses the same phrase autobiographically when saying that for nearly three years he did not mount the cushion outside the two meal-times. Qianshan Shengren gives the phrase an institutional edge: before ordination, he says, even the two daily meals count as stolen food. The headword names actual scheduled meals before it carries any quoted contrast.

Senses.Explanation: Mixing mud with water pictures substances losing a clean boundary; Chan speakers use the image in appraisals, answers, and paired formulas with differing verdicts. In a recasting of three phrases, "understanding from the first phrase" is called "mixing mud and blending water," followed by "binding oneself without a rope" and "landing with all four edges on the ground" (第一句薦得，和泥合水；第二句薦得，無繩自縛；第三句薦得，四稜著地). Another record groups it with "speaking a dream without a dream" and "not knowing good from bad" (無夢說夢，和泥合水，撒屎撒尿，不識好惡). Yet the phrase also stands as a direct answer to "what is the true source of the great road?" (如何是大道真源), and one discourse pairs "where wind cannot enter" with "mixing mud and blending water" in both directions. Another contrasts failing to mark the moment, when black and white remain undistinguished, with marking it too late, called "mixing mud and blending water." These are different recorded placements of one image. The texts do not supply the uniform gloss “descending to the student's level,” so neither does this entry.

Senses.Explanation: Master Zhigong is the pre-Zen figure whom Chan records quote, identify with a direct answer, and place in exchanges at Emperor Wu's court. His name occurs 494 times in 133 texts. Asked "what is buddha?" Wanan Daoyan answers, "Master Zhigong" (誌公和尚); when challenged, he says, "Zhigong is not an idle monk" (誌公不是閑和尚). In the Fu Dashi case, Fu mounts the seat, strikes the desk once, and descends; Zhigong asks Emperor Wu whether he understands, then says, "the great man has finished lecturing the scripture" (大士講經竟). Later masters repeatedly quote and criticize that verdict. His sayings are also treated as named textual material: the Twelve-Hour Song, Fourteen Sections, and Great-Vehicle Praises. Zen therefore deploys Zhigong as a named answer to "what is buddha?," court interlocutor and adjudicator of Fu Dashi's action, and quoted author.
